# The Moon That Runs Away

## Scripture
*"Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence? If I go up to the heavens, you are there; if I make my bed in the deep, you are there."* — Psalm 139:7–8 (NIV)

## Reflection
November's moon often rises late and races across the sky, seemingly fleeing before the dawn. To the ancients, it must have felt like something untamed—waning to a sliver, vanishing entirely, then swelling back to fullness. Yet every phase is held in perfect gravitational partnership with the earth. The moon never truly escapes; it simply follows an orbit it cannot break.

We have our fleeing seasons too. When grief or doubt presses in, we may feel like we're running from God—through busyness, through silence, through the dark. But the psalmist knew the truth: there is no sky so high, no night so deep that God is not already there. We do not orbit away from His presence; we orbit within it. Like the moon, our dimmest phases are still held by a faithfulness we cannot see.

The Hebrew word for sky, *shamayim*, appears in this psalm twice—"up to the heavens." And yet God is there. The moon's phases are not failures; they are faithful rhythms. So are ours. Perhaps this fall, when the moon hides its face, let it remind you that even in your darkest phase, you are held in an orbit of grace that never lets you go.

## Prayer
Lord, when I feel far from You, remind me that Your presence is the very sky I move through. Hold me in Your faithful orbit, even in my dimmest nights. Amen.
